subject: Geography
central_question: How are India’s land resources used for agriculture, how do farming systems and crop patterns vary, and what problems and development strategies shape Indian agriculture?
in_scope_units: Land-use categories recorded by the land revenue department and the distinction between reporting area and geographical area
Changes in India’s land use between 1950–51 and 2019–20 and their economic causes
Common Property Resources and their importance for rural livelihoods
Agricultural land use, total cultivable land and cropping intensity
Cropping seasons in India: kharif, rabi and zaid
Types of farming: irrigated, rainfed, dryland and wetland farming
Foodgrains, cereals and pulses, including rice and wheat
Oilseeds, fibre crops and other crops including cotton, jute, sugarcane, tea and coffee
Agricultural development after Independence, including irrigation, HYV seeds and the Green Revolution
Problems of Indian agriculture, including monsoon dependence, low productivity, indebtedness, fragmented holdings and underemployment
Environmental problems of agriculture, including soil degradation, waterlogging and salinisation
banned_topics: Detailed river-basin water-resource management, which belongs to the Water Resources chapter
Detailed mineral belts and energy resources, which belong to the Mineral and Energy Resources chapter

known_pitfalls.claim: Area classified as forest is always the same as actual forest cover.
known_pitfalls.correction: The chapter distinguishes recorded forest area from actual forest cover; recorded forest area may rise without an equal rise in actual cover.

known_pitfalls.claim: Net area sown and gross cropped area mean the same thing.
known_pitfalls.correction: Net area sown counts the physical land cultivated, while gross cropped area counts all crop sowings, including land cropped more than once.

known_pitfalls.claim: Dryland farming means farming without any rainfall.
known_pitfalls.correction: Dryland farming occurs mainly in areas with annual rainfall below 75 cm and depends on moisture conservation and drought-resistant crops.

known_pitfalls.claim: Agricultural development after Independence removed all regional and social problems.
known_pitfalls.correction: The chapter records gains in output but also continuing problems such as monsoon dependence, low productivity, unequal land distribution and environmental degradation.

recommended_example_progression: Use NCERT Exercise 2(ii) to distinguish net sown area from gross cropped area.
Use NCERT Exercise 2(iii) to explain why increasing cropping intensity matters in a land-scarce, labour-abundant country.
Use NCERT Exercise 2(v) to compare dryland and wetland farming.
Use NCERT Exercise 3(i) to organise the environmental problems of land resources.
Use NCERT Exercise 3(ii) to connect post-Independence agricultural strategies with their achievements and limitations.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The chapter ends with EXERCISES 1–3: five MCQs, five short-answer questions and two long-answer questions.
